issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Contamination/feeling dirty is much more characteristic of sexual trauma than a mugging/robbery. In a robbery case it is not impossible, but without any corroborating interpersonal violation, bodily disgust, or related threat/memory content, this item is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me
issues.explanation: Emotional closeness as a trigger is difficult to link to the stated trauma type of mugging/robbery and to the rest of the profile. The other triggers, threat items, and memory content point to danger/safety and coercion themes, whereas this item implies an intimacy/interpersonal-betrayal theme that is not represented elsewhere.

vignette: Priya had been completing her morning deliveries when the man in the faded leather jacket pulled up alongside her idling sedan. He did not ask; he simply reached through the open window, gripped her shoulder, and forced her to hand over her phone and the insulated delivery bag. Being forced to do something had left a permanent mark on her, and the sudden pressure against her collarbone became the anchor of what followed. When officers arrived, the presence of police pulled her back to that window, their questions piling up until she could barely explain that she was fine. She told herself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, a quiet reassurance that helped her push through the early weeks. Yet the memory did not fade into abstraction. She remembered the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment was a picture in her mind: the man’s raised hand, the phone slipping from her fingers, the red taillights blurring as she watched him walk away. When these memories surfaced, she sometimes heard things in her head that she had heard during the frightening event—the scuff of boots on asphalt, the metallic click of her car door. Other times, there was no image at all. Sometimes she felt the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, a sudden wave of dread that filled her chest while she stood behind the counter at the pharmacy, waiting for her change. As months passed, her avoidance took root in the routines of her delivery work. She avoided driving, and even being a passenger in a vehicle felt like a concession to uncertainty. She picked up drugs to smooth the edges of her days, watching her route deliveries accumulate on the kitchen counter as the weeks blurred. In the driver’s seat and on the city sidewalks, she learned to read the street differently. People acting suspiciously no longer passed her unnoticed; a pedestrian’s quickened pace or a stranger’s lingering glance felt like a quiet signal that the threat was still out there. She always identified escape routes before she felt comfortable anywhere, stepping into shops and waiting at crosswalks with her eyes tracking the exits. Her mind refused to let her rest. She woke during the night to check whether she was safe, her hand resting on her chest as she listened for footsteps or the rustle of branches against her window. She remained unable to relax even when she knew she was in a safe place, her shoulders staying braced on her familiar sofa as though expecting the door to open again. The work environment made her internal landscape visible. Colleagues laughed over shared coffee breaks, but she felt isolated and set apart from others, disconnected by a quiet certainty that something could break her routine without warning. She would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened, replaying the moment not as a stranger’s random act, but as her own failure to act. She could not stop bad things from happening to her; no matter how carefully she planned her routes or checked her mirrors, the city felt inherently unpredictable. Her avoidance had tangible costs. Friends stopped inviting her out when she canceled last-minute, and her delivery earnings dipped as she turned down the longer routes. She told herself repeatedly that she had been safe all along, yet her body refused the reassurance. Now, at twenty-two, Priya finds herself at the clinic doorway during her lunch break, still wearing her high-visibility vest. She has come because the unpaid invoices are stacking up and the quiet of her evenings no longer feels quiet at all. What she fears most is not another robbery, but the slow erosion of her own agency; what she hopes for is a way to sit in the passenger seat without bracing, to trust that her stillness is not a failure, and to finally let her chest unclench.
